title: Caring for the sick
hookLine: a sign-up sheet nobody fills, and a sick monk the Buddha washes with his own hands
tomorrow: pain that won't leave: fight it, or breathe with it?

cards: A meal sign-up goes around for a neighbor home from the hospital, and the slots sit empty while everyone assumes someone else will take them.
The monastic rules tell of a monk sick with dysentery, lying in his own filth, with nobody tending him. The Buddha walks in with Ananda. He brings water.
The Buddha pours, Ananda washes, and together they lift the monk onto a bed. Then the Buddha asks the other monks why no one had cared for him.

teach.b: The monks answer: he was of no use to us. And the Buddha says: you have no mother or father here to care for you. If you don't care for one another, who will?
Then the line the story is remembered for: whoever would care for me, let him care for the sick. Now, inside the tradition, a real question follows: whose job is the care?
One view, from this very story, puts it squarely on the community. The rule that follows names who must tend a sick monk, his teacher, his companions, and if no one, the whole sangha.

teach.h: VIEW ONE: THE CARE IS OWED.
teach.b: On this view, care is owed, fully, and nobody gets to say not useful to us.

teach.h: VIEW TWO: THE PATIENT HAS A SHARE.
teach.b: Another view, from a short pair of suttas, says the patient has a share too.
A sick person is easy to care for, the Buddha says, when they do what helps, know the right measure, take their medicine, tell the nurse honestly how they are, and bear the pain patiently.
And a good nurse gives care out of kindness, not for gain, without disgust, and can lift the patient's spirits with a word of Dhamma. The first view guards the sick from being dropped.
The second guards the carer from being crushed, and treats the patient as a person with work of their own. Both stand in the same texts.

how: Caring for the sick is a recognized duty in Buddhist monasteries, where rules name who must tend a sick monastic; lay Buddhists often visit the sick, bring food, and chant or sit with them.

games.q: what does “caring for the sick” mean?
o: a duty that belongs only to doctors and nurses
praying for a cure instead of giving medicine
tending someone ill, as the Buddha did with his own hands

games.q: the sick monk and two views — tap the pairs.
p: said he was no use to them
washed him and laid him on a bed
the patient has a share of the work

s: the Buddha left the sick monk's care to others
he brought water and washed him with Ananda's help.
the suttas describe what makes a patient easy to care for
doing what helps, taking medicine, reporting honestly, bearing pain.
in the texts, a good nurse cares in hope of a reward
a good nurse cares out of kindness, not for gain.

games.q: your mom says caring for grandpa is all on the family, whatever he does. your aunt says he has to help himself too. state your aunt's best case.
o: she just wants to do less work and is making excuses.
the suttas say a patient who takes medicine and speaks honestly is easier to help; that keeps carers from being crushed.
she's right and your mom is wrong; the texts only give the patient's side.
games.why: both views are in the texts: the Vinaya says the sick must be cared for, and the suttas describe a patient's share. the aunt's best case is the second.

practice: Think of one person who is sick or worn down right now, near or far. Write them a short, warm message, no advice, just that you're thinking of them, and send it if it feels right.
Then rest with the breath and let the care sit with you.

wordCard.voice: Caring for the sick: the care the Buddha gave with his own hands, owed by the community and shared, where it can be, with the patient.

orig.note: Pali: gilanupatthaka, one who attends the sick, a nurse.

carryVoice: The line that stays: care for the sick, as if caring for the Buddha. Four of nine.

sources.ref: Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga 8.26 (the monk with dysentery; the Buddha and Ananda wash him; 'whoever would attend on me should attend on the sick'; the rule on who must nurse a sick monk)
Anguttara Nikaya 5.123-124 (five qualities of a patient easy to nurse; five qualities of a good nurse)
